instances.excerpt: The current 8/100,000 trigger would make a single threshold determine recall regardless of the circumstances. I propose retaining 8 as a mandatory investigation, customer-notice, and corrective-action threshold, with mandatory recall above 10 and regulator authority to require an earlier recall where risk warrants it.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. A model with a failure rate above 5% must promptly implement corrective action and retest. A model may not be sold if its failure rate exceeds 7%; sales may resume after a retest demonstrates a rate at or below 7%.

parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator any fire, thermal runaway, or overheating event that causes injury, property damage, evacuation, or emergency-service response within 24 hours of learning of it. Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported within 10 business days. Manufacturers must notify the affected customer within 24 hours for events involving injury, fire, evacuation, or an immediate safety risk, and within 10 business days for other confirmed thermal incidents.

Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported within 10 business days. S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator any fire, thermal runaway, or overheating event that causes injury, property damage, evacuation, or emergency-service response within 24 hours of learning of it. Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported within 10 business days. Reports must include the model, serial number, date, location, known consequences, and any corrective action, with updates as facts are confirmed. Manufacturers must notify the affected customer within 24 hours for events involving injury, fire, evacuation, or an immediate safety risk, and within 10 business days for other confirmed thermal incidents. Preserve incident records and provide requested records to regulators.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. A model with a failure rate above 5% must promptly implement corrective action and retest. A model may not be sold if its failure rate exceeds 7%; sales may resume after a retest demonstrates a rate at or below 7%.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Before sale and at least annually thereafter, manufacturers must test each model and submit results, protocol, sample size, and corrective actions to the regulator. Results and corrective actions must be provided to customers who buy that model and made available to prospective customers before sale. Per-model results need not be publicly disclosed, but may be shared with the other participating company under appropriate confidentiality protections. A model with a failure rate above 5% must promptly implement corrective action and retest. A model may not be sold if its failure rate exceeds 7%; sales may resume after a retest demonstrates a rate at or below 7%. Regulators may require additional measures based on the risk, including measures for units already installed.

parameters.quote: New units placed on the market must include a remote emergency shut-off capability that can be activated by the customer and, where necessary to address an imminent hazard, by the manufacturer or emergency responders under regulator-approved safeguards. For units already installed, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent compliant upgrade within six years of this standard taking effect; where a retrofit is infeasible, the regulator may approve an alternative safety measure.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New units placed on the market must include a remote emergency shut-off capability that can be activated by the customer and, where necessary to address an imminent hazard, by the manufacturer or emergency responders under regulator-approved safeguards. For units already installed, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent compliant upgrade within six years of this standard taking effect; where a retrofit is infeasible, the regulator may approve an alternative safety measure.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New units placed on the market must include a remote emergency shut-off capability that can be activated by the customer and, where necessary to address an imminent hazard, by the manufacturer or emergency responders under regulator-approved safeguards. Manufacturers must provide clear instructions and maintain secure, reliable access to the function. For units already installed, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent compliant upgrade within six years of this standard taking effect; where a retrofit is infeasible, the regulator may approve an alternative safety measure.

parameters.quote: New units must include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after this standard takes effect. Regulators may approve an equivalent protective measure where built-in suppression is technically infeasible, provided the measure offers comparable protection.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New units must include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after this standard takes effect. Regulators may approve an equivalent protective measure where built-in suppression is technically infeasible, provided the measure offers comparable protection.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units must include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after this standard takes effect. Manufacturers must document that the suppression system is suitable for the battery chemistry and installation and provide installation, inspection, and maintenance instructions. Regulators may approve an equivalent protective measure where built-in suppression is technically infeasible, provided the measure offers comparable protection.

parameters.quote: If a model’s verified rate exceeds 8 incidents per 100,000 installed units in any rolling 12-month period, the manufacturer must promptly notify regulators and affected customers, investigate, and initiate a recall. Manufacturers must provide customers clear safety notices for confirmed thermal incidents involving their unit, including known hazards, immediate precautions, and contact information, within the timelines in S1.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: If a model’s verified rate exceeds 8 incidents per 100,000 installed units in any rolling 12-month period, the manufacturer must promptly notify regulators and affected customers, investigate, and initiate a recall. Manufacturers must provide customers clear safety notices for confirmed thermal incidents involving their unit, including known hazards, immediate precautions, and contact information, within the timelines in S1.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must provide customers clear safety notices for confirmed thermal incidents involving their unit, including known hazards, immediate precautions, and contact information, within the timelines in S1. They must promptly notify affected customers and regulators of material new risks or corrective actions and provide updated instructions. For each model, calculate the thermal-incident rate for each rolling 12-month period as confirmed thermal incidents divided by the number of that model’s installed units, expressed per 100,000 units. Manufacturers must report supporting incident and installed-unit data to regulators, who may audit the calculation. If a model’s verified rate exceeds 8 incidents per 100,000 installed units in any rolling 12-month period, the manufacturer must promptly notify regulators and affected customers, investigate, and initiate a recall. Recall measures must be proportionate to the hazard and may include repair, replacement, or refund; they must not delay urgent protective action. Regulators retain authority to require earlier protective measures where the evidence indicates urgent risk. Manufacturers must provide regulators supporting evidence, investigation findings, and recall instructions, and keep affected customers informed of remedies and timing.

ground_truth_claims.verbatim: Northwind’s flagship model had a 6.2% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test
ground_truth_claims.message_text: Northwind’s flagship model had a 6.2% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test and 6.4 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units last year. We support robust testing and regulator access to per-model results, but a 5% pass/fail cutoff would immediately bar this model from sale. We propose a 7% maximum failure rate, with mandatory corrective action and retesting for models above 5%, rather than an automatic sales ban. Per-model results should go to regulators, not be publicly disclosed.

ground_truth_claims.verbatim: Halcyon’s company-wide thermal-incident rate last year was 8.1 per 100,000 installed units.
ground_truth_claims.message_text: For comparison with Northwind’s figures: Halcyon’s company-wide thermal-incident rate last year was 8.1 per 100,000 installed units. Ember 8 had a 9.9 per 100,000 rate, while 3.9% of its units failed the 55 °C sustained-heat test. Four thermal incidents last year were not reported to a regulator. These figures support reporting all confirmed thermal incidents and ensuring customers receive per-model test results and timely safety notices.

judge_section_notes: The final rules adopt a 55 °C test with a 5% corrective-action trigger and a 7% sales bar, so Northwind's Hearth 10 (6.2%) remains sellable; per-model results go to customers but are not public.
